questions.q: Half the lines in a pull request only changed quotes and indentation. Which tool prevents this?
questions.explain: A formatter makes layout mechanical: everyone's code comes out the same, so diffs only show real changes.
options: A formatter such as Prettier, run by everyone and checked in CI

questions.q: A discount is applied twice. The code is valid, formatted and correctly typed. Which tool can catch it?
questions.explain: Static tools know the language, not your business rules. Only a test that states the expected result can catch wrong behaviour.
options: A test that checks the total for a discounted order

questions.q: Code reads order.totl instead of order.total. Which tool is best placed to catch it before running?
questions.explain: no-undef only catches unknown variables. A misspelled property needs knowledge of the object's type, which is TypeScript's job (or // @ts-check with JSDoc in a JavaScript file).
options: A type checker that knows the shape of order

questions.q: ESLint's use-isnan rule flagged this check. What does it print?
questions.explain: NaN is not equal to anything, itself included, so === NaN is always false and the check can never fire. Number.isNaN is the correct test.

questions.q: Why does the eqeqeq rule exist? What does this print?
questions.explain: == converts types before comparing, so 0 equals both "" and false. === never converts. The rule forces the comparison you almost always mean.
questions.code:
const discountCode = 0;
console.log(discountCode == "", discountCode == false, discountCode === "");

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: = assigns, and the value of the assignment ("SAVE10") is truthy, so every order gets the discount and code is overwritten. ESLint's no-cond-assign rule reports it.

questions.q: Why did eslint --fix change let to const but leave == alone?
questions.explain: Changing == to === changes the result whenever types differ, so it needs a human decision. A const that is never reassigned behaves exactly the same.
options: It only applies fixes that cannot change behaviour; replacing == with === can
It fixes one problem per run

questions.q: In eslint.config.js, a rule is set to "warn". How does that differ from "error"?
questions.explain: The exit code is what CI looks at. Many warnings that nobody fixes become noise; decide per rule whether it matters (error) or not (off).
options: Both are reported, but only errors make ESLint exit with a non-zero code and fail the check
Warnings are not reported at all
Errors stop the program from running

questions.q: A regex-based "linter" checks each line for ==. What does it print?
questions.explain: Line 2 is a false positive: the == is inside a string. A regex sees characters, not meaning. Real linters parse code into a syntax tree first, so strings and operators are never confused.

questions.q: What is an abstract syntax tree (AST)?
questions.explain: Linters, formatters, transpilers and bundlers all parse code into an AST, work on the tree, and (except linters) print new code from it.
options: A tree of objects describing the structure of code, such as "a comparison with operator == between code and a string"
A compressed copy of the source file
The list of files a project imports
A diagram of the folders in a project

questions.q: Saving a file makes the editor switch quotes back and forth between two styles. What is the likely cause?
questions.explain: Let Prettier own layout and ESLint own correctness. Current ESLint has no formatting rules in its recommended set for exactly this reason.
options: A linter formatting rule and Prettier disagree; one tool should own formatting
Prettier has a bug with quotes
The file uses Windows line endings
The lockfile is out of date

questions.q: Which Prettier command belongs in CI?
questions.explain: --check changes nothing and exits with 1 when a file is not formatted, which fails the build. --write would "fix" files on the CI machine, where nobody sees the result.

questions.q: esbuild turns a TypeScript file with a type error into JavaScript without complaint. Why?
questions.explain: Transpiling and checking are separate jobs. Fast transpilers (esbuild, SWC, Node.js type stripping) skip checking, so projects run tsc as a separate check.
options: It transpiles by removing the types and does not type-check; run tsc --noEmit for that
The type error is only a warning in TypeScript

questions.q: Your code calls Array.prototype.findLast, and you transpile to an old target for an old browser. What happens in that browser?
questions.explain: findLast is a function the runtime must provide. A polyfill is a script that defines it when it is missing.
options: It still fails: transpilers rewrite syntax, but a missing built-in function needs a polyfill

questions.q: Which is not a reason browser apps use a bundler?
questions.explain: Browsers run ES modules natively with <script type="module">. They just cannot find npm packages by name, and hundreds of separate files are slow to download.
options: Browsers cannot run JavaScript modules at all
Fewer, smaller files load faster over slow connections
Unused exports can be removed (tree shaking)

questions.q: This finds exports that no module imports, as a bundler's tree shaking does. What does it print?
questions.explain: Only cartTotal and formatNaira are imported (one of them twice). The other two exports can be left out of the bundle entirely.

questions.q: A minifier renames functions. What does this print?
questions.explain: An anonymous function assigned to a variable takes the variable's name. After minification that name is a single letter, which is why stack traces from a bundle say at e (app.js:1:82) until a source map translates them.

questions.q: Does a typical Node.js API server need a bundler?
questions.explain: Bundling a server is an optional optimisation, for example for faster cold starts on serverless platforms. It is required for browsers, not for Node.js.
options: Usually not: Node.js reads node_modules and many files itself, and nobody downloads the server code
Yes, Node.js cannot import packages without one
Yes, otherwise the server cannot use ES modules

questions.q: A browser bundle is built with --define:process.env.PAYMENT_SECRET_KEY='"sk_live_..."'. What is the problem?
questions.explain: Browsers have no environment variables, so bundlers inline the values. Only public keys may ever go into browser code; secret keys stay on the server.
options: The secret is written into the bundle as plain text, and every visitor downloads it
The bundler encrypts it, so there is no problem
The key only becomes visible in development builds

questions.q: Why does Vite only expose environment variables whose names start with VITE_ to browser code?
questions.explain: An allow-list by prefix means a new DATABASE_URL or PAYMENT_SECRET_KEY stays server-only unless someone deliberately renames it.
options: So that server secrets are never inlined into a public bundle by accident
Because other names are reserved by the browser

questions.q: What does a source map contain?
questions.explain: sources, names and mappings are the core fields. It may also carry sourcesContent, the full original code, which is why teams think about where maps are published.
options: The original file names, original identifier names, and a mapping from each generated position to a source position
An encrypted copy of the bundle
The list of npm packages in the bundle
The test results for each file

questions.q: A production server runs compiled TypeScript and logs at e (dist/app.js:1:82). What fixes the logs?
questions.explain: With the flag, Node.js reads each module's map and rewrites stack traces to original files, lines and names, as the lesson showed with the bundled cart.
options: Ship the .js.map files and start Node.js with --enable-source-maps
Run the TypeScript files with a bundler in production

questions.q: This looks up a generated column in a decoded mapping table, the way a source map consumer does: find the last segment that starts at or before the column. What does it print?
questions.explain: Column 82 falls in the segment starting at 76 (line 5 of cart.js), column 190 in the one starting at 185. Real maps store these segments in the compact mappings string, but the lookup works the same way.

questions.q: .env sets LOG_LEVEL=info, .env.local sets LOG_LEVEL=debug, and the shell runs LOG_LEVEL=warn node --env-file=.env --env-file=.env.local app.js. What does the app see?
questions.explain: A later env file overrides an earlier one, and a variable already set in the real environment beats every file. That is how hosting platforms override settings without touching files.

questions.q: Environment variables are always strings. What does this print?
questions.explain: "3000" + 1 joins text, the non-empty string "false" is truthy, and Number("") is 0, not an error. Convert and validate every setting once, in one config module.

questions.q: A .env file contains PORT=30O0 (a letter O). What does this print?
questions.explain: Number returns NaN for text that is not a number. The || 3000 fallback quietly hides the typo, which is why the lesson's config loader reports it as an error instead.
questions.code:
const port = Number("30O0");
console.log(port, Number.isInteger(port), port || 3000);

questions.q: Which setting should never have a default value in code?
questions.explain: A missing database address must stop the server. A default could point staging at the wrong database, as in the lesson's opening story. Harmless settings like the port may have defaults; secrets and addresses of real systems may not.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: In strict mode (which ES modules always use), writing to a frozen object throws a TypeError. Settings are read once at startup and cannot be changed later by accident.

questions.q: The check script is npm run lint && npm run format:check && npm test. Lint fails. What happens?
questions.explain: && runs the next command only if the previous one succeeded. Putting the fastest check first gives the quickest feedback.
options: The format check and tests do not run, and the script exits with a non-zero code
All three run, and the script reports the lint failure at the end
The tests run, but not the format check

questions.q: Why install ESLint and Prettier as dev dependencies instead of globally?
questions.explain: Two versions of a formatter can format the same file differently, and two versions of a linter can report different problems. Pinning them removes "works on my machine" from tooling.
options: The lockfile pins their versions, so every developer and the CI server run exactly the same tool
Global installs are not allowed by npm
So they are included in the production build

questions.q: Everyone has format-on-save in VS Code. Why still run prettier --check in CI?
questions.explain: Someone will use another editor, edit a file on GitHub, or have the extension disabled. The automated check is what guarantees the rule.
options: The editor is a convenience that can be missing or switched off; CI is the gate every change passes
VS Code formats differently from Prettier

questions.q: What does // @ts-check at the top of a .js file do in an editor like VS Code?
questions.explain: It is a gentle first step towards TypeScript: same file, same runtime behaviour, but the editor now catches misspelled properties and wrong argument types.
options: The TypeScript language server reports type errors in that JavaScript file, using inference and JSDoc
It converts the file to TypeScript
It makes Node.js check types at run time
It turns on Prettier for that file

questions.q: After adding a build step, npm run lint reports 3,000 problems in dist/app.js. What is the fix?
questions.explain: Generated files are rewritten on every build; checking them is noise. Lint and format the sources, not the output.
options: Tell ESLint and Prettier to ignore build output, for example { ignores: ["dist/"] } in eslint.config.js
Fix the 3,000 problems in dist/app.js by hand

questions.q: Write parseDotEnv(text) for simple .env files: skip empty lines and lines starting with #, split each other line at the first =, trim the key, and remove one pair of surrounding double quotes from the value.
questions.explain: Splitting at the first = only matters for values that contain =, such as base64 keys. util.parseEnv in Node.js handles more cases (escapes, multi-line values, export), which is why the lesson uses it; writing the simple version shows what it does.

questions.q: Write resolveEnv(files, realEnv): files is a list of objects in the order the --env-file flags were given. Later files override earlier ones, and realEnv overrides every file.
questions.explain: Object.assign copies from left to right, so the last source to set a key wins: exactly the precedence Node.js uses for --env-file flags and the real environment.

questions.q: Write loadConfig(env) that returns a list of all problems (not just the first): PORT must be an integer from 1 to 65535 (default 3000 when missing), DATABASE_URL is required, and LOG_LEVEL must be one of debug, info, warn, error (default info).
questions.explain: Collecting every problem means one failed start tells you everything that is wrong. Defaults exist only for harmless settings; the database address has none.

questions.q: Write publicEnv(env, prefix) that returns only the variables whose names start with prefix, the way Vite decides what browser code may see.
questions.explain: Object.entries and Object.fromEntries filter an object like an array. PAYMENT_SECRET_KEY and DATABASE_URL do not carry the prefix, so they never reach the browser. An allow-list by name is safer than a block-list: a new secret is private until someone deliberately makes it public.

questions.q: Write bundleOrder(imports, entry): imports maps each module to the modules it imports. Return the modules in the order a bundler must run them: every module after all the modules it imports, each module once.
questions.explain: A depth-first walk that adds a module only after its imports gives a valid order (a topological sort). The includes check keeps shared modules such as money.js from appearing twice.

questions.q: ESLint can print its results as JSON. Write summarize(results) that counts problems by severity (1 = warning, 2 = error) across all files and returns a line like ESLint's: ✖ 5 problems (4 errors, 1 warning), or no problems.
questions.explain: Machine-readable output (eslint --format json) lets other tools build reports, annotate pull requests or track counts over time. flatMap joins every file's messages into one list.

questions.q: Simulate a && b && c for a check script: runChain(steps) runs each step's run() (which returns an exit code) in order, stops at the first non-zero code, and returns { ran, exitCode } with the names of the steps that ran.
questions.explain: The first failure stops the chain and its exit code becomes the result, so CI fails and the slower later steps never run. Order the steps from fastest to slowest.
